p.src: A founder eventually has to stop asking only, How do I get better? and ask, Who can we build with? Lecture 109 adds that missing people-selection layer. The interview question is direct: when building a company or launching a venture, what traits make someone worth bringing onto the team?

p.src:
The answer begins with role fit. People have natural lanes. One person may look like a sales type, another like an engineering type, another like an operations type: $\operatorname{RoleType}(c)
\in
\{\text{sales},\ \text{engineering},\ \text{operations},\ldots\},$ where $c$ is a candidate for the team. That first classification matters. A company needs people who can actually contribute somewhere. But the speaker does not let role fit become the whole decision: $\operatorname{RoleFit}(c)
\nRightarrow
\operatorname{Hire}(c).$ A useful lane is evidence, not a verdict.

p.src: Can talent, school, referrals, or prior success substitute for character inside an early company?

u.src: Can talent, school, referrals, or prior success substitute for character inside an early company?
en: Can talent, school, referrals, or prior success substitute for character inside an early company?

p.src: No. The speaker’s distinction is blunt: skills can be taught, but traits cannot be reliably changed. In book terms, talent is only usable when the person can receive correction, keep learning, and persist through difficulty.

u.src: No. The speaker’s distinction is blunt: skills can be taught, but traits cannot be reliably changed. In book terms, talent is only usable when the person can receive correction, keep learning, and persist through difficulty.
en: No. The speaker’s distinction is blunt: skills can be taught, but traits cannot be reliably changed. In book terms, talent is only usable when the person can receive correction, keep learning, and persist through difficulty.

p.src:
The non-negotiable trait set named in the interview is: $\mathcal{T}
=
\{\text{coachable},\ \text{humble},\ \text{persistent}\}.$ The hiring screen is therefore not merely is this person impressive? It is: $\operatorname{TraitClear}(c)
=
\operatorname{Coachable}(c)
\land
\operatorname{Humble}(c)
\land
\operatorname{Persistent}(c).$ Only after that screen does visible ability become operationally useful.

p.src:
The sales example makes the rule concrete. A person may be the strongest sales rep at a generic XYZ company, and the speaker grants that this shows talent. But it still does not prove success here: $\operatorname{Talent}(c)
\lor
\operatorname{School}(c)
\lor
\operatorname{Referral}(c)
\nRightarrow
\operatorname{SuccessHere}(c).$ This creates a useful tension with the earlier sales chapters. Lecture 112 says experience cannot be Googled; lecture 179 says sales should be practiced and reviewed. Lecture 109 adds the condition underneath both claims: the person must be teachable enough for practice to work and humble enough for experience to correct them.
